progressionInfo.name: 12-Bar Blues Progression
progressionInfo.subtitle: The foundational form that shaped blues, jazz, rock & roll, and modern popular music - a twelve-measure harmonic pattern that tells a complete musical story.

properties.label: Structure
properties.value: Three sections of four bars each

properties.label: Form
properties.value: Creates complete harmonic journey with turnaround leading back to beginning

examples.label: Blues
examples.value: The foundation of Delta and Chicago blues

chordDiagrams.title: Basic 12-Bar Blues in E
chordDiagrams.description: The most common key for blues guitar. These three dominant 7th chords form the foundation of the blues.
practiceNotes: E7 for bars 1-4, A7 for bars 5-6, E7 for bars 7-8
B7 for bar 9, A7 for bar 10, E7 for bar 11, B7 for bar 12 (turnaround)
Focus on maintaining a steady shuffle feel throughout

chordDiagrams.title: Blues in Key of A
chordDiagrams.description: Another popular key for blues guitar with easy open chord shapes.
practiceNotes: Very comfortable chord shapes for open position
Great for practicing with a shuffle rhythm

advancedApplications.title: Guitar-Friendly Keys
advancedApplications.description: The 12-bar blues works best in certain keys on guitar.
items: Key of E: E7 - A7 - B7 (most common blues key)
Key of A: A7 - D7 - E7 (great for open position)
Key of G: G7 - C7 - D7 (open position friendly)
Key of C: C7 - F7 - G7 (jazz-inflected blues)

advancedApplications.title: Rhythm Patterns
advancedApplications.description: Essential rhythm feels for playing the 12-bar blues.
items: Shuffle Feel: Swing eighths (triplet feel) - the classic blues groove
Basic Strum: Down-up pattern with consistent rhythm
Emphasis: Strong accents on beats 1 and 3
Muting: Use palm muting for a tighter, more controlled sound

advancedApplications.title: Quick Change Variation
advancedApplications.description: The quick change adds the IV chord in bar 2, creating more harmonic movement early on.
items: Bars 1-4: I - IV - I - I (IV appears in bar 2)
Bars 5-8: IV - IV - I - I (same as standard)
Bars 9-12: V - IV - I - V (same turnaround)
Creates more harmonic interest in the opening section

advancedApplications.title: Jazz Blues Substitutions
advancedApplications.description: Jazz musicians add sophisticated substitutions and extended harmony to the blues form.
items: ii-V substitutions in various measures
Chromatic passing chords (#IVdim7)
Extended chords (9ths, 11ths, 13ths)
Tritone substitutions
Minor blues variations (i-iv-V)
Modal interchange chords

practiceCategories.title: Week 1: Foundation
items: Master E7, A7, B7 chord shapes
Learn the basic 12-bar structure by heart
Practice clean chord transitions between I, IV, and V
Work on steady rhythm with a metronome
Count bars out loud as you play through the form

practiceCategories.title: Week 2: Feel & Groove
items: Develop the shuffle feel (swing eighths)
Practice with a metronome at various tempos
Add the quick change variation
Learn the 12-bar blues in the key of A
Work on dynamics - louder during the V chord section

practiceCategories.title: Week 3+: Application
items: Play along with classic blues recordings
Learn the form in multiple keys (E, A, G, C)
Try jazz blues substitutions
Develop your personal blues style and phrasing
Practice turnarounds and intros

notatedExercises.title: Basic 12-Bar Blues in E
notatedExercises.description: The standard 12-bar blues form using dominant 7th chords in the key of E. Each chord is played as a whole note per measure.
practiceNotes: Bars 1-4: E7 (tonic section - establishing the key)
Bar 12: B7 (turnaround - leads back to bar 1)

notatedExercises.title: Quick Change Blues in E
notatedExercises.description: The quick change variation moves to the IV chord (A7) in bar 2 instead of staying on the I chord, adding more harmonic interest to the opening.
practiceNotes: Notice the A7 in bar 2 - this is the 'quick change'
Compare the feel with the standard version
Many classic blues songs use this variation

notatedExercises.title: Jazz Blues with Substitutions in C
notatedExercises.description: A jazz-influenced version of the 12-bar blues featuring chord substitutions, passing chords, and extended harmony.
practiceNotes: C7 - F7 - C7 - C#dim7 - F7 - F7 - C7 - Am7 - G7 - F7 - C7 - G7
Notice the chromatic passing chord (C#dim7) in bar 4
The Am7 in bar 8 adds a ii-V feel leading to the turnaround
Practice each substitution slowly before putting it all together

ii-V-I: Jazz substitutions commonly applied to blues

sections.title: Blues Scales
items: Minor pentatonic scale - the primary blues scale
Blues scale (minor pentatonic + flat 5th)
Major pentatonic for a brighter sound
Mixolydian mode over each dominant 7th chord

sections.title: Genre Applications
items: Blues: The foundation form for all blues styles
Jazz: Standard vehicle for improvisation
Rock: Basis for countless classic rock songs
Country: Used in country blues and western swing

sections.title: The 'Axis of Awesome' Connection
items: While many pop songs use I-V-vi-IV, the 12-bar blues remains the foundation for understanding harmonic journeys
The blues form teaches tension and resolution in its purest form
Learning the blues form builds harmonic awareness that applies to all genres
The turnaround concept (bar 12) is foundational to understanding musical form
